Reference [16]. The fifth observation is that the peak load
magnitudes are similar for resonant responses whether
acquired with uniform flow or an ABL. This observation was
unknown and is perhaps the most significant finding
presented in this report. It has long been theorized that
turbulence and a velocity profile could prohibit the
establishment of organized and nearly-discrete vortex
shedding [2]. However, the data presented here indicate that
uniform flow testing is not overly conservative and that
organized vortex shedding can indeed occur in the presence
of turbulence and a significant velocity profile.

There are three uniform flow data points in the vicinity of 100
ft/s that appear to be outliers in Figure 17 where uniform flow
produced notably larger dynamic response. However, these
three points occurred at slightly higher velocities than the
ABL counterparts for the same azimuth angles. This is
apparent when analyzing the response segregated by azimuth
angle regions. Peak bending moment due to lift acquired at a
series of wind azimuth angle regions are shown in the
appendix as Figure A1. Two of the three outlying points are
readily apparent in the East and Southeast azimuth regions.
Therefore, the dynamic response acquired in uniform flow
and an ABL is likely more similar than a casual review of
Figure 17 would otherwise indicate.
Maximum Resultant Loads—The maximum resultant
bending moment was computed as the maximum of the root-
sum-square of the base bending moments about the Y- and Z-
axes for a given time history data record. This component is
also illustrated in Figure 14. Maximum resultant bending
moment acquired in an ABL and uniform flow are shown in
Figure 18, and the values acquired at a series of wind azimuth
angles are included in the appendix as Figure A2.
Comparison of the maximum resultant bending moment to
the other components previously mentioned reveals that the
majority of the maximum load incurred during resonant
events is a result of dynamic loads due to lift.

Loads Acquired with a Proprietary Model—As previously
discussed, testing was also completed with a proprietary
model. The details of the model cannot be released; however,
comparative data can be shown if normalized by arbitrary
constants. Static bending moment due to drag, peak bending
moment due to lift, and maximum resultant bending moment
are plotted in Figures 19, 20, and 21 respectively for the
proprietary model tested at 60% of flight Reynolds number.
The same arbitrary constants were used to normalize velocity
and bending moment, respectively, thereby enabling a
response comparison between data acquired in uniform flow
or in an ABL.
Similar to the observations made for the research model, the
static bending moment due to drag has comparable
magnitude with uniform flow and with the ABL. Specific
azimuth region comparisons are also available in the
appendix as Figure A3.
